gamma flip.def: The level of the index at which estimated net dealer gamma crosses zero, so that dealer hedging damps moves on one side of it and amplifies them on the other. Vendors give it other names, and some define nearby levels of their own that are not the same thing.

call wall.def: The strike at which a gamma exposure model places the largest concentration of call gamma. Some traders read one above the price as resistance.

put wall.def: The strike at which a gamma exposure model places the largest concentration of put gamma. Some traders read one below the price as support.

destabilizing gamma.def: The negation of published gamma exposure, used in the effective-volatility formula: positive when dealers are net short gamma and their hedging amplifies moves, negative when they are net long gamma and it damps them.

effective volatility.def: The volatility prices show once dealer hedging feeds back into them, as opposed to the volatility news alone would cause. Feedback from short-gamma hedging raises it and feedback from long-gamma hedging lowers it.

gamma squeeze.def: A rally driven by dealers buying the underlying to hedge calls they have sold, whose deltas rise as the price rises, so that each purchase lifts the price and forces the next.

short interest.def: The number of a company's shares that have been sold short and not yet bought back, often quoted as a percentage of the public float. It can exceed 100% because a borrowed share, once sold, can be lent and shorted again.

short covering.def: Buying back shares previously sold short, to close the position. When many short sellers cover at once, their buying adds to a rally.

hedge flow.def: The trades in the underlying that dealers must make, summed across all of them, to keep their books neutral to direction as the price moves. It opposes a move when dealers are net long gamma and joins it when they are net short.

sign convention.def: The rule a gamma exposure model uses to decide whether dealers are long or short each option, since open interest counts contracts but not who holds them. The two best known give calls and puts opposite signs, and differ from each other in every sign.

JPM collar.def: The quarterly index-option position of JPMorgan's Hedged Equity Fund, which holds stocks, buys a put spread below the market and sells calls above it. It is one of the few large index-option positions whose holder is public.

demand-based option pricing.def: The theory that end users' net demand for options moves their prices, because dealers who cannot hedge perfectly charge for the risk left in the positions they absorb. It helps explain why index puts are expensive and the skew is steep.

Open-Close data.def: Cboe's files of option volume split by the type of trader (customer, professional customer, broker-dealer or market maker), by buy or sell, and by whether each trade opened or closed a position. It is the main source on sale that shows who holds SPX options.

trade classification.def: Inferring whether a trade was a purchase or a sale by the party that started it, from its price against the quotes, against the previous trade, or both, when the data do not record the side. Standard rules get a sizable share of option trades wrong.

autocallable.def: A structured note that pays a coupon and is redeemed early if the index is above a set level on a check date, and exposes its holder to losses if the index falls through a lower barrier. The issuing bank hedges it by trading the index and its options.
